✋ *Everyone keeps repeating the same polite myth — **_“AI won’t take your job; it’ll just change it.”_* Cute. But here’s the part the video refuses to drag into the light: *we still get chained to an eight‑hour workday even when the machines have already eaten half the workload.* Look at the FX industry. Every new tool — motion capture, procedural generation, Houdini, real‑time rendering — was supposed to *_“free artists.”_* Instead, studios used the efficiency to *tighten deadlines, inflate expectations,* and *slash budgets.* Workers didn’t get shorter days; they got *longer crunch, more shots, more revisions,* and *less pay.* Automation didn’t liberate them. It *weaponized them.* If AI does 50% of the grind, they don’t send you home early — they widen their jaws. They demand the remaining 50% twice as fast, with a smile, with a KPI, with a *_“great opportunity for growth.”_* The elevator operator vanished, the airline pilot multiplied, sure — but the worker’s hours stayed nailed to the floor. Because the workday was never about output. It was about *obedience,* about keeping you in the ritual, in the chair, in the cage. The video shows how technology expands jobs. Fine. But it doesn’t show how the *hours never shrink,* how the cage never opens, how every _“productivity gain”_ becomes a fresh layer of expectation. FX proves it: the better the tools get, the more brutal the schedule becomes. Machines get better. Work gets lighter. But your time — your life — stays locked at eight hours, because the system isn’t hunting efficiency. It’s hunting *compliance.* AI doesn’t replace you. 🥷 *It just sharpens the teeth of the structure that already owns your day.*

Why is everyone leaving the tech job market? Good question asked and I will try to explain from my past computing experiences. The reasons why most of us leave the tech job is because of the technological demanding changes that comes along the way. Before you can learn it, the next waves of change comes in. The company send us for refresher courses hoping to embrace the new technology fast. But to my surprised, even the course trainers are struggling to learn the new things and teach you at the same time. To cut the story short, this means studying by yourself all the latest thick reference books, e-learning hours, mugging, experimenting, playing around, write > 1,000 lines logic (mapping crazy if then else situations), solving the problem only realised the software bugs itself causing the issue. Last straw that breaks the camel back, they found someone better who knows about it and you're not required anymore. From my past IT experiences, its better to look for jobs that can requires strategic know how skills that can add values to the company growth. E.g. How to implement computer information technology (e.g. BI tools) to help your company maintain a strategic marketing edge over your bench marked competitors. How to put in system (e.g. ERP / ORP) that can standardised work procedures and at the same time monitor, improve man power hours (to remove duplication job process)and reduce operation costs. What I am trying to say skills that can help you grow as someone sitting in the CEO / COO / CIO / consultants / managerial / technical /etc position. Just imagine you have the right skills to go into any company and help to improve the ways of doing things in the fast paced changing environments ( e.g. Artificial Intelligence / Cloud Computing / Biometrics / Block Chains / E Commerce : G2B, B2B, B2C To Mobile Commerce - anything on-line transactions based / etc). Lastly, I will leave all the nitty gritty details (nuts and bolts) to my energetic technical friends out there. Work smart and real hard as a beginner learning the ropes, know when to call it a day (quit) and quickly move on to another level up there.
